description: Frog stretch for inner thighs, hips and pelvic floor relaxation: how to do it safely, what to feel, common mistakes, easier and harder versions.
intro: The frog stretch is a deep inner-thigh stretch done on all fours with your knees wide. It opens the hips and the muscles around the pelvic floor. It is a relaxation and mobility move, not a strengthening one, and fits best at the end of a session.
feel: You should feel a strong but tolerable stretch along your inner thighs and hips as you move your hips back, with your belly and pelvic floor soft. You should not feel sharp groin pain, knee pressure or your lower back sagging. Self-check: if you cannot breathe slowly and calmly, bring your knees in a little.

mistakes.wrong: Spreading the knees as wide as possible right away
mistakes.right: Start a little wider than your hips and widen slowly over several sessions.
Keep a natural curve and rest on your forearms if that helps. Hips and spine move back together.

mistakes.wrong: Bouncing in and out of the stretch
mistakes.right: Move slowly and pause. Small, slow rocks are fine, but no bouncing.

easier: Pad your knees, keep them closer together and stay on your hands. You can also stretch one side at a time.
harder: Lower onto your forearms, widen the knees a little and hold toward a minute. No squeezes; the point is release.
who: Useful for people with tight inner thighs from running, cycling, lifting or long sitting.
skip: Skip it or keep the range small if you have knee or groin pain, a hernia, recent hip, groin or abdominal surgery, or are pregnant or postpartum and not yet cleared. A pelvic floor physiotherapist can help with pelvic pain or a very tight pelvic floor. Stop if it hurts.

faq.q: Is the frog stretch good for the pelvic floor?
faq.a: It can help the area around the pelvic floor relax and move better. It does not strengthen the muscles, so use it alongside gentle Kegels, not instead of them.

faq.q: Why do my knees hurt in the frog stretch?
faq.a: Hard floors and too wide a position are common causes. Pad your knees, bring them closer and keep your ankles in line with your knees.
